In so far as this mill is concerned, I would certainly urge upon

I think every Canadian will say that we should have a plate-producing mill in Canada somewhere, and if we are to have it at all I 'think we should have it in connection with one of the big institutions of that class. The biggest steel-producing plant in Canada to-day is the Dominion Steel Corporation. There may be bigger ones later on, but at the present moment that is the largest in Canada producing steel of the very best class, as has been shown by what they were supplying during the war and what they have been doing in rail production. I think the Dominion Steel Company have produced as good a rail as is produced anywhere on the American continent. It was well understood last year, and I think it is still understood, that the Government were to build that plate mill and that arrangements had been completed for that purpose. The mere fact that a difference has arisen in price one way or the other is not a sufficient reason to disturb the policy agreed upon by the Government, considering that the production of steel plates within our own borders is such an important matter to the whole country. These plates are to be produced at tide water. The mill willlje within a stone's throw of tide water of Sydney harbour, from where both coasts and inland by rail can be supplied. The ships are to be built in Halifax, and by steamers from the shores of Sydney harbour to Halifax the transportation of these plates is not a difficult proposition. It would be better, one would think, if both were going on at the same place, and the natural place for shipbuilding would be Sydney harbour, but the Government have decided otherwise, and they having so decided, I have no criticism to offer. But I certainly think it would be a retrograde movement to abandon the idea of producing these plates, and I trust the minister will determinedly carry forward the policy upon which he launched in connection with the erection of a mill. I am glad to find that Mr. Workman, president of the company, has met him in a conciliatory and businesslike spirit on that point, and I hope that nothing will interfere with an advanced programme in connection with shipbuilding and the furnishing of facilities for producing plate within our own country.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am very glad indeed to hear from the leader of the Opposition the words of commendation that he has been good enough to utter in regard to the contract made between the Government and the Dominion Steel Corporation to manufacture two hundred and fifty thousand tons of ship's plate. The best price for the Government that could be agreed upon over a year ago' was $4.15 per hundred pounds, based upon the price at which steel billets were selling at that time, viz: $25.50 per ton. Hon. members no doubt are aware that ship's plates are made from steel billets, and in talking with the president of the company I learned that steel billets would not in any event decline in price more than $10 a ton. When the Government entered into that contract with the steel corporation it was as a war project; as I stated in the House yesterday you could not get steel from the United States; and notwithstanding the fact that we had placed an eighty thousand ton contract there, we were only able to obtain six thousand tons. Other countries at war, such as Britain and France were depending on the United States for stqgl, and Japan was also getting steel from that country. The United States, having a huge mercantile marine programme themselves to carry out, naturally were going to serve their own necessities first before they supplied the needs of others; therefore, to make shipbuilding a self-contained industry in Canada, and to enable this country to get ships during the period of the war, it seemed to the Government that there was no other course open but to enter into the best contract we could to have the steel plates made here. It is greatly to the credit of the steel corporation that they were able to place before the Government a more favourable proposal than we could get from' the United States. Another thing in its favour, and which is gratifying from a patriotic point of view, is that the ore used by the steel company to make the pig iron originates in British territ'ory, and comes from Newfoundland, so that all the materials used in production are obtained on British soil. But after the armistice had been signed, the price of ship's plates being 2| cents in the States, against possibly a minimum price of $3.75 under the Dominion Steel Company's contract and the Government 'being obligated to take no less than fifty thousand tons per year for a period of five years, making two hundred and fifty thousand tons in all, it seemed to my colleagues and 
to me that we could not very well afford to pay that price. The arrangement looked very favourable a year ago when plates were selling at from four to ten cents a pound, but it does not look so favourable now.
I quite agree with the leader of the Opposition that to make Canada's shipbuilding programme permanent, the industry must be on a self-contained basis in this country, and that we ought to make our own ship's plates. I am quite satisfied that the Dominion Steel Corporation could carry out the contract, and I am also well satisfied that Sydney is a very good point at which to make these plates. No definite conclusion has yet been arrived at, but the company fairly stated that if they had completed their plant and installed the machinery necessary it would have been at a capital cost of 15,000,000. Therefore, if they are to meet the American price it would take them many years before they could do so, and possibly they might never be able to write off the initial cost ol the plant, or a portion of it. If the Steel Company would give us a more favourable price, the Government would be more inclined to go on with the proposition than it is to cancel it. If, however, the company cannot see their way clear to modify the price, I think it is in the best interests of the country to cancel the contract.

The minister has told us
that the Government has only received delivery so far of six thousaiid tons out of the eighty thousand tons contracted for. I understood him to say yesterday that the contract with the United States was based on a price of 31 or 31 cents per pound?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Replying to the hon. member yesterday, I had the privilege of informing him, in regard to the forty-five ships under contract for the Dominion Government, that the prices were based, not on the contract made with the Dominion Iron & Steel Company, but on the agreement made with ithe United States at 3J cents per pound. I also stated yesterday that the Steel Corporation had not imported any of the required machinery at all. All they have done so far has been to partially erect the building; it contains no plant in the way of machinery, engines, and boilers.

It is possible to take another view of the question which has been touched on by the minister and by the leader of the Opposition as to the wisdom of importing steel plates if the object is to build ships successfully and profitably. I remember hearing Mr. Lloyd George address a very enthusiastic audience in the Old Country and he was meeting the argument that had been advanced at that time, which was some .years before the war, that free trade was hurting Britain because certain steel plates had been imported from Germany to Barrow-in-Furness. I am sure this Committee would listen to Mr. Lloyd George upon such a question with interest, and possibly with instruction. Mr. Lloyd George said that the person who complained of those steel plates coming ito Barrow-in-Furness didn't know quite enough about 'his subject, and he pointed out that Sir Hugh Bell, one of the greatest iron-masters in the north of England, had taken the trouble to trace the history of the steel plates after they arrived from Germany at Barrow-in' Furness. It is quite true, said the great statesman, that those steel plates came to Barrow-in-Furness from Germany, but Sir Hugh Bell traced what happened to them, and it was extremely interesting, Mr. Chairman, as showing how the Old Country succeeded in shipbuilding. He said those steel plates came from Germany, and they enabled a firm of ship builders to take a contract for shipbuilding at Barrow-in-Furness against the world's competition. They converted Germany's steel plates, which they bought cheaply, into ships, and sold the
steel plates in the form of ships back to Germany at a handsome profit. Well, that didn't seem a bad transaction-to employ the highly paid shipbuilding industry of Great Britain at Barrow-in-Furness upon the half finished articles of the less well-paid artisans of Germany, put them into ships and sell them, against the world's competition, back to the country that had sold to Britain the cheap steel plates. I merely mention this incident to show that it is possible to take a contrary view to that which has been expressed by my hon. friends on opposite sides of the House. It is possible to take that contrary view and to hold it very strongly if we look to the interests of Canada instead of to some provincial interests which may be helped by the spending of money locally.

There is a disposition in this country to urge provincial interests, but I think national interests and wide economic interests should be more especially regarded. It will suit a particular case sometimes in order with considerable cunning to draw a general conclusion, but it is a practice that must be guarded against. We are not here for the purpose of being beguiled by any such form of reasoning. The fact of the matter is that if you lay down the proposition that has just been outlined, you must also lay down the proposition that cheap products and cheap labour shall have free access to this country. The result would be that you would ruin production and reduce the producer to the level of the foreigner. That is the true general conclusion to be drawn from such a statement. In the particular instance which has just been developed it may quite reasonably have occurred just as outlined; but, as I say, to draw a general conclusion from it is both dangerous and harmful.
We cannot do anything of the sort, if we wish to develop Canada. I might say in particular that if you put a Chinese wall seven hundred feet high around this country and balanced consumption and production, you might well raise this country to the highest possible degree of economic equilibrium, which any man who knows anything about the science of economy is aware is quite possible. But he would also know that if you reduce that wall, if you disturb the equilibrium and destroy the balance of your own resourceful country by admitting cheap labour and cheap labour's products, you must ultimately reduce the country and the people to the level of China and the Chinese coolie.
How does my hon. friend propose to get his ships over his seven hundred foot wall?

I might answer my hon. friend by saying that in the case I supposed we would not need to get them over the seven hundred foot wall. That is just where the error of such reasoning as my hon. friend's comes in. We would have the ships employed within our own country; they would get all the employment they required. We would have the farmer raising no more than was necessary for the sustenance of the people, and we would have the manufacturer making no more than was necessary for their requirements, and we would have the administration employing its arts for preserving the admirable balance of trade in this country. Then we would have such complete immunity from confusion that there would be plenty of time to study economic subjects and bring into this House better conclusions than we have just heard announced.

There is no doubt that there are two sides to every question. I have no doubt that in order to build up any country its resources should be developed first to the fullest possible extent, and if we can have further expansion to permit of export, so much the better. But my good friend from Red Deer has been telling me lately that he is devoting a great deal of his attention to the reading of the Holy Writ, and I am sure in that sphere of study he will find no writer more congenial to his close reasoning than the Apostle Paul. He talks to me about provincialism and sectionalism. But if he will read Paul he will find that the Apostle tells us that we are members one of another. Paul says, "Will the eye say to the nose, 'I am not of the body because I am not the nose'? Will the hand say to the foot, 'I am not of the body because I am not the foot'?" Paul reasons that out and concludes that we are members one of another, and of the one body. That magnificent philosopher of former days has many points in common with my good friend from Red Deer and yet sufficient divergency of view to be distinguished from him, and I am sure we will be safe in following Paul's reasoning. And when I advocate the manufacturing of plate at Sydney Harbour it is not because Sydney Harbour happens to be close to my home town in the Gem of Canada, the province of Nova Beotia. I had nothing to do with the 
placing of that contract, I was not consulted; the Government of this country- and among the many things of which I accuse them I do not include sectionalism- in their wisdom selected Sydney as the place where those plates should be manufactured. All I am asking is that they shall continue to implement their decision.
While I am not a very high protectionist, I am not in favour of the tremendous wall that my friend from Peterborough would like to build; but I cannot help knowing that protection of certain industries has done much for this country. I cannot help knowing that in connection with this very plate industry we are talking about and the institution of the steel works at Sydney those steel works have furnished a market for our Nova Scotia coal and employment for thousands of colliers who to-day would not be employed were it not for the assistance which the Government in the early stages gave to the development of our steel and iron industry.
Now, if there is to be a further development of that industry and of the coal industry by the manufacture of plate and the building of ships in this country, I think that it is a wise move. I do not think any one is preaching any political hearsay when he advocates the development of whatever resources we have within our own country and making ourselves as far as possible self sustaining and independent. I have no doubt the day is not far distant when we shall harve a navy of our own, and I want this country to be able to build its own warships, from stem to stern, with what we can ourselves produce. That is the policy I wish to advocate. As I said, I ram not a high protectionist, but I am prepared to deal with facts and circumstances and not with any theory which may suit .somewhere but not elsewhere.

I despair of ever getting the last word with my hon. friend, but as we are in Committee perhaps I may be allowed to say that I do not think the fact he has produced to us is very strong evidence in support of his theory.
I do not know the exact number of the inhabitants of Sydney. I hope they are numerous, and I should like to see the population of that town grow, but I should like to see it grow by a reasonable interpretation of the Apostle Paul's language and not by an unreasonable interpretation of it. Of course, I do not believe in a body which does not look after both the hand and the foot. What I object to is

a body that would be so unreasonable as to endeavour to clothe its foot with the glove of the hand. That is what protection does, and it is not very successful in the operation. I come from a part of Canada where we have some larger towns than Sydney. Winnipeg, for instance, is quite a city compared with Sydney; it has grown in a shorter time, and it has grown on products raised by people who are men enough to raise them against the competition of the world and who want no protection. The same is true of Calgary, Edmonton, Regina, and the other numerous cities of the West which will go on to be larger cities than Sydney is to-day. Pap-feeding never made a man and it never made a province. It is with men as with nations-people who stand on their own feet are in the end always the strongest, and I should like my hon. friend to take a leaf out of this book of economic sense and not confine his studies absolutely to the scriptures; because, after all, the scriptures were not made to teach either political economy or astronomy. The hon. member knows they get very far wrong on astronomy.

Would the minister take into consideration, when he is building these ships, the wisdom of establishing a few of them on our Upper lakes in order that we may be able to control freight rates. In 1909, wheat was brought from Port Arthur to Montreal for cents a bushel, while last year, steamships on our Upper lakes charged eleven cents for carrying wheat between those two ports, and the rates are constantly increasing, {lespite the fact that 6ince 1909 we have been spending millions of dollars on our waterways.
Would the minister also take into consideration the fact that the Canada Steamships Company, a company that is now capitalized at $30,000,000, went in a merger in 1912 whereby six or seven companies merged together, and they invested only some $6,000,000 or $7,000,000 of actual capital, but they floated that company with $12,000,000 of watered stock, $12,000,000 of preferred stock and $6,000,000 of bonds. What has happened? That company have increased the rates and have practically a monopoly of traffic on our inland waiters, and they are in this position to-day that no.t only are they paying seven per cent on their preferred stock and bonds, but this year they started to pay four per cent on their $12,000,000 of common stock. In addition to that, they have set aside $5,000,000 of a
surplus. This merely goes to show the need oif some effort to control the rates, tolls and tariff agreements in connection with our ' boats on our inland waters. Therefore, when the minister is taking into consideration the building of ships entirely, as I understand, for ocean traffic, which is badly in need of regulation as well, I hope he will consider the advisability of building ships to be placed on our inland waters in order that we may be able to control freight rates there.

What was the effect on merchant shipping in the United States? In a comparatively few years after the Civil war, the United States did not carry 10 per cent of its own exports and imports in its own bottoms. Let me give another practical illustration. We, who believe in the principle of freedom of commerce, are always being attacked as having splendid ideas but as not being practical folk. In the few years before the war our enemy, Germany, had succeeded in building up a very substantial mercantile marine. How did she do it? By building her ships under free trade conditions. The German. Government arranged their fiscal policy in such a fashion that everything that went into a ship built in Germany, although Germany was a highly protected country, went in free, and on no other basis could Germany have challenged Great Britain as the mistress of the seas.
Mr. MiIDDLEBRO: Did not Germany, in addition to that, subsidize shipbuilding in order that ships might be built more cheaply than in England?
' Mr. IMoMAiSTER:	Possibly. I am not
prepared to say " yes " or " no " to that question, but no subsidy that Germany could have given, could have offset the handicap German shipbuilders would have been under, had they had to build ships under protectionist conditions.
Mr. M.IDDLEBRO: Does the hon. member not admit that a subsidy is the highest and worst form of protection?
Mr. MdMASTEfi: No, a subsidy is not the worst form of protection. Subsidies are honest and tell the people what they are paying in order to assist some special interest in the country. One of my great objections .to granting special privileges to some classes of the community at the expense of the whole is that the people do not know in that case what they are paying, while under the bonus or subsidy system they have some idea what is being paid out. I would respectfully submit to the minister that nothing less than disaster will meet any plan of shipbuilding, ship-owning or ship-operating if it is not upon a basis to meet competition from all over the world. I know the minister will listen to what I say with courteous attention, and I only trust that he will follow my suggestions.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Answering, first, the hon. member (Mr. G-. E. Armstrong), who asked if it was the policy of the Government to have ships on the Great Lakes, I am happy to say that that is a part of our policy. We intend to have ships, not only on the Pacific and the Atlantic, but on all the principal trade routes, and certainly on the Great Lakes, so that our transportation chain will be complete.
In answer to the hon. member for Brome, I would have been disappointed if he had made any different speech from that which he did make. We both come from the same city, we are both very good friends, each of us respects the views of the other, but on this question we are certainly very far apart. He would have Canadians simply hewers of wood and drawers of water. Canadians have demonstrated that with the very moderate protection we have had in this country for a number of years they can hold their own with the people of any other country in the world. I am sorry the hon. member was not in his seat yesterday, when I explained to the Committee that Canadian yards have turned out ships equal in design and efficiency, and in every other respect to ships built in any part of the world. A few years ago some people in this country thought that ships could not be built in Canada, but it has been amply demonstrated during the last two years that ships can be built here successfully. If my hon. friend had been here yesterday he would have learned that, according to the opinion of Sir George Hunter, of the famous shipbuilding firm of Swan & Hunter, ships built in England, Ireland and Scotland at the present time are costing three times as much as ships built in pre-war times. No one believes for a moment that wages in the United Kingdom will ever reach again the low level prevailing before the war. Both skilled and unskilled labourers in the Old country are asking for a higher rate of wages, and I think they are perfectly justified in doing so. In view of the marvellous development that has taken place in Canada during the last few years, and the skill which Canadians have exhibited in turning out ships equal to similar ships turned out in the yards of the United Kingdom, I take issue with my hon. friend when he says that Canada will not be able to compete with the United Kingdom and other shipbuilding nations. As I stated yesterday, between now and the next session we are going to consider if it will be necessary to render any aid to our shipbuilders when the days of keen competition arrive, and

there will, be plenty of time to deal with this matter at the next session of Parliament.	/
My hon. friend has referred to the United States and apparently he has not kept abreast of the times. The United States has constructed 555 steel ships of various kinds and tonnage. Chairman Hurley, of the United States Shipping Board, states that they are going to build 1,136 more ships, and that when their entire mercantile marine programme has been completed they will have the enormous tonnage of 16,000,000 tons. The United States Government are going to aid that vast mercantile fleet. With a fleet like that next door to us, my hon. friend's advice to the Government is that we should sit down with folded arms and go out of the shipbuilding business. That is not the policy of this Government.

I never said that the Government should go out of or continue in the business. I laid down as a principle that ydu could not have a successful shipbuilding or ship operating business except on a basis that would meet competition from all the world.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I accept my hon. friend's correction. I think I am correct in inferring from his remarks that he did not think Canada would be able to compete with other countries. 1 take issue with him there. When the time comes i think Canada, [DOT]probably with some small assistance from the Government, will be able to compete with all other countries.

At the risk of wearying the Committee, I should like to supplement the very interesting reference of my hon. friend from Brome to the case of the United States by a single figure. In the year 1861 the shipping tonnage of the United States was two-and-a-half millions, and the tonnage of Great Britain and Ireland four-and-a-quarter millions. At that time, as my hon. friend has very correctly said, Americans were very generally crossing the seas in American bottoms, and American shipping bade fair to become the greatest in the world. In 1910, after fifty years of free trade in Great Britain and fifty years of protection in the United States, the two-and-a-half million tons of the United States had sunk to one-and-a-half million tons, and the four-and-a-quarter million tons of Great Britain had risen to nearly twelve million tons. I think those figures are a perfect demonstration 144
of the truth of the argument of my hon. friend from Brome.
The minister is still extremely enthusiastic about this shipbuilding programme, and I should like to add just one word more from practical experience to induce him to be cautious about going too far in this business. What happens to shipping in war time is no guide whatsoever as to the safety of a shipping policy in times of peace. I was indirectly interested in shipping in Great Britain during the Boer war, and ships about which I had complete knowledge, from my indirect interest, were paying dividends of twenty per cent. Within a very few years of that war, and during some period of it, the ships that were before paying twenty per cent were paying only a nominal dividend, of one to one-and-a-half per cent. I think those facts -and they are facts-about the United States on the one hand, and drawn, on the other, from my own personal experience of British shipping in and after the Boer war ought to make the minister cautious. *

I have no desire to
enter into a discussion of the respective merits of protection and free trade, but I can scarcely forbear to say a word or two on behalf of the policy that the Minister of Marine has introduced. I am very strongly in favour of supporting all the industries of Canada, and as we used to be a great maritime nation I see no reason why we should not in the near future resume the high position we held forty or fifty years ago as compared with the other nations of the world. Some three or four years ago I waited on the then Minister of Naval Service and begged him to embark on a policy such as my hon, friend brought forward yesterday and has before us to-day. At that time my appeal fell on deaf ears. Had the policy been inaugurated three or four years ago, and had we ships afloat during the last two years of the war, if those ships had made two or three successful trips across the Atlantic they would have paid for all that they would have cost at that time. In my judgment, we did not embark on that policy early enough, but because the policy is a little tardy in coming that is no reason why we should not now endorse it.
One compensation has come to me this afternoon in the splendid tribute paid to this policy by the leader of the Opposition. I feel sure that the Maritime Provinces cannot go back on the shipbuilding industry. No one who has been in the House during the last three or four years and heard



the appeals of the present Lieutenant-Governor of New Brunswick (the Hon. William Pugsley), will fail to remember that day in and day out for weeks at a time he reiterated the desirability of embarking on Just such a policy as the Minister of Marine has now introduced. Canada is largely a maritime nation. The Great Lakes are the greatest body of fresh water in the world, and the tonnage that passes through the Sault Canal is probably the heaviest that passes through any canal in the world. Is not that a strong reason why we should have ships of our own on the Upper lakes to take care of the wheat traffic from the West, and to furnish the necessary competition to railways? Our western farmers cannot get wheat to market unless they have cheap shipping on the lakes. It is an absolute necessity of the situation that wre should have competition between boats and railways to get the best effect on freight, and that leads to a profit to the farmer of the West of several cents a bushel more than he would receive if his wheat had to depend upon our railways to bring it out. That is the point I desire our western friends to consider in looking at this naval programme. I am rather sorry for the hon. member for Brome, because he is an exceedingly decent fellow. He has told us that hi.s
4 p.m. father was a seafaring man.
Well, I cannot accuse my hon. friend of any seafaring propensities, but I may tell him that in his tariff and trade ideas he has been at sea ever since he entered public life. I think he will appreciate that remark, because if the policy he proposes were followed, not only would we have no shipbuilding, but we w'ould have no other industries to speak of in this country. As I said, I do not want to be drawn into an argument with regard to free trade and protection, but I want to tell my friend that it behooves him to prepare for the Budget debate which will come on in the near future, and in the meantime I will give him a problem as suggested by Abraham Lincoln, who was one of the fathers of protection in his day and generation, now fifty years ago. I would like my hon. friend to make a note of this problem and bring in a solution when he comes to discuss the question on the Budget. Abraham Lincoln made this statement: "If you want a ton of pig iron and you buy it from a foreign nation, you have got your ton of iron but you have parted with your money. But if"-

Of course-

Hold on; let me state the whole problem. "But if you dig that iron from the ground and produce it in your own country you have your ton of pig iron and you have your money." If my hon. friend can overthrow that doctrine I hope he will bring us the solution when the Budget debate comes up. In the meantime, I say both hands up for this shipbuilding policy. It means work and high wages for the labouring men of Canada, and I can tell my hon. friend (Mr. McMaster) that he has done very well to-day in informing us he is not opposed to all manner of encouragement to industry. The light will burn better in the window for his having made that statement, I am sure. I may say, and this I know to be true, that I have lying on my desk in my office in this Parliament building petitions from 3,800 working men of the city of Brantford in favour of a protective policy and no serious changes in tariff, and what I have is only a sample of what is coming to others. The -workingmen know that their bread and butter is bound up in sustaining the industries of Canada, and this is really a basic industry which the minister proposes. While it is true that prices on shipping are high at the present time, and while perhaps we cannot compete with Great Britain, I know the minister is very near the mark when he says that Britain is not ' going to build more ships in the near future at such prices as have obtained in the past. This is a good time for us to get in. The war has sunk about twelve to fifteen million tons of shipping and the question naturally is, who will make that up? The nations of the rvorld will replace that shipping, and why should not Canada take its part in this work? Mow is the time to embark on a shipbuilding policy so that Canada may step into the breach, and with her ability as she has shown in the war, I feel absolutely certain that Canada can put ships on the water that will make as good speed and carry cargoes just as cheaply and safely as any other nation in the world. She may not be able to do it quite as cheaply at the outset as she will later on, but once establish the yards, get skilled men into them and get the engine producing factories and all the other necessary appliances, and a nation like Canada that has produced more than half the shrapnel fired by the British armies in the war need have no fear that the same energy, intelligence and good policy that have been pursued in the past will lead to a triumph in shipbuilding, and that we will have a fleet on

the waters both inland and on the oceans to carry our traffic to all the nations.

I do not intend to enter into a controversy as to the advisability of either protection or free trade, but there is one point favourable to shipbuilding in Canada to-day which I think has not been brought out properly and which it is worth while to bring to the attention of hon. members. I refer to the matter of selling the wheat crop of Canada next year. The hon. member who has just taken his seat, mentioned traffic on the lakes. I wish to take up a different point and one that is important at the present time to the wheat growers of the West. The United States has fixed the price of wheat for this year in that country. For that reason they are going to have probably the biggest wheat crop in the history of the United States and the United States will also probably lose a great deal of money by paying these prices to the farmers. For the same reason she will make her greatest effort to unload that wheat upon the grain markets of the world which are European markets, particularly British. She will endeavour to sell that wheat in the European markets, in the past few years export Canadian wheat has been shipped to Europe and 65 per cent of it, or two-thirds of the wheat we have exported has been exported through American ports. Suppose the United States this year came to the conclusion that they had plenty of wheat to supply the markets in Europe. They are expecting to have four to five hundred million bushels for export. Suppose they say that having plenty of wheat to ship and having fixed the price of wheat they are going to oppose any Canadian wheat going through the American ports; in other words they would block the export of 65 per cent probably of our wheat unless we are able to supply shipping to export it. tin view of that situation, it seems to me that this point is one of the most important that should be taken into consideration in a shipbuilding programme. There is no doubt that these ships will cost a great deal, perhaps much more than they would cost in the British shipbuilding plants, but I believe we should take into account, in considering this matter, the possibility of exporting the wheat of Canada. I may be asked the question, will these ships be built in time to handle this year's crop? One year's crop is usually shipped the following year, or a very great deal of it. I desired to bring this matter to the attention of the Committee because I did not hear 1441
it mentioned before. I believe the Minister of Marine referred to it but he did not elaborate it sufficiently to explain the point I wish to make.

Cargo vessels
of the United States are privately owned, with the exception of a few that have been built by the Government within the last year or two. All these ships that have been built by the Government are now to fall into private hands. It has never been the policy of the United States except for war vessels to have a fleet of cargo vessels belonging to the United States Government in so far as I can learn and, if it is true that the ships in the United States are to be placed in the hands of private own-' ers, my hon. friend if he will give half a cent a bushel more than market rate for carrying the wheat of Canada to the markets of the world will get the whole fleet of the United States to carry it. They will take the wheat without caring whether it was grown on the prairies of Western Canada or of the United States. They are looking for freight for their ships and they will go wherever the freight is best. The fact that the Canadian Government own their ships will not help the western farmers because the western farmer will have to pay the market price for carrying his wheat and there are always ships to carry wheat in normal times. In fact, there were so many of them that before the war they were carrying wheat for nothing. Wheat was going over as ballast because the rates were so low. That happened then; will happen again. Rates go up and down like anything else. The time will come when there will be enough cargo vessels to do the world's business and they will cut prices. That is only one of the laws of economics.	.;
I do not' think that the fact that the Government owns the ships will help very much. It is not helping at the present time. Attention has been called to the fact that the few vessels that we now have, owned by the Government, are not developing Canadian trade. They are developing the trade of the United States. A cargo vessel has to take business where it can get it. An illustration was given of the case of the Voyageur. The Voyageur took a cargo from Halifax to the West India islands. When she reached the West India islands I suppose she found that there was no cargo suitable to bring back to Halifax. But she got a cargo of sugar for New York.

She loaded the sugar and took it to New York. I am not complaining about that but I am pointing out to my hon. friend and the minister the absurdity of expecting to run these cargo vessels in the way that it is proposed that they shall be run as Government vessels and expecting that the western farmer will reap a benefit from their operation.

There are two points against the argument which the hon. gentleman has advanced. In the first place, as the hon. gentleman states, while vessels may be privately owned in the United States, the United States will control these vessels and make them sail as they like. That is the first point. In the second place, the hon. gentleman savs that half a cent a bushel difference on wheat will bring the ships where we wish to bring them. I do not think that is correct. Ships go to United States ports for the reason that they have western bound cargoes. There is much more traffic from Europe to the United States than to Canada and that has been the great reason in * the past why Canadian wheat has been shipped by United States ports. The fact that they could get cargoes at half a cent a bushel more would not draw these ships to Canadian ports for the reason that they would have to come light. Therefore, the ships owned by the Government would be used under the circumstances.

If my
hon. friend's ship is in Boston or New York it would not be very far to move her back to a Canadian port. There is no necessity, because she sailed from a Canadian port, of her coming back to a Canadian port. That is not the way shipping is carried on. I was going to refer to the contract with the Dominion Steel Company. I have not any particular or definite views on that contract because I have not studied it. But I have seen it stated that it is somewhat improvident. I do not say that a contract of that kind could not be justified on the ground that we are starting a new industry. I think that, as a free trader, I might take that ground. We had a very good illustration in the steel business. Sonne time ago we had no steel business in Canada. The Government was very anxious that something should be done to establish the steel business in Canada and the solution was a bounty. A bounty was paid to the steel industries for a number of years, decreasing year after year. That bounty was granted in order to establish

the steel industry at Sydney, Hamilton and various other places. It cost us about $20,000,000. That was regarded, at that date, as a very large sum of money. It is only regarded as a bagatelle to-day. But I suppose there are very few men in Canada to-day who would want to go back to the old condition of no steel industry in Canada and get back the $20,000,000. They-thought it was a good, progressive move and it has paid the country. On the same ground I would oUggest that we might establish a plate-mill in Sydney by giving a certain amount of help. I agree with my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) that a bounty of that kind, when we know what we are paying, is far less objectionable than a protective duty. We understand that we are going to put up so much money and that is why I asked the minister to tell us just what we were expected to pay.
I suppose that he is able to make a calculation that if we carry out this contract that has been made with the Dominion Steel Company, it would cost us a certain amount of money and it would be satisfactory to know how much it is going to cost us.
But the main point in regard to the shipbuilding industry is that we must make it attractive to private capital. Although the Dominion Government is going into shipbuilding and ship owning, if Canada is going to find a place on the sea it must be as a result of the investment of private capital. The Government can usurp certain things. The Government if lit chooses to pay the price can own a certain number of ships, but the Government cannot build up a great shipbuilding industry unless the people will invest their money in it and become interested in it. It is only a makeshift for the 'Government to go in for the owning of cargo vessels. I am not a prophet but I would not be afraid to prophesy that the Government will not stay very long in the business.
I would not be surprised if in ten years the Dominion Government were out of the business although the people of the Dominion of Canada will not be out of it. The people of Canada will go into the business and stay in it. Has the Government any plan to remedy the handicap that every one admits exists? Man after man has spoken in this debate and every one has stated the same thing; that we cannot build vessels in Canada to compete with vessels built in Great Britain. For this condition of affairs has the Government a solution? I would like to know what

the minister intends to do to remove that handicap and to enable private enterprise in Canada to go into this business, make it a success, and compete with the rest of the world.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Of course the Government believes that shipbuilding will be a permanent industry in -this country. I may say that if the House passes the Supplementary Estimates that I shall bring down in the very near future to have a limited number of ships constructed in addition to the forty-five we have under contract, for the reasons that I gave to the Committee yesterday, the cost of these ships will be very materially less than the cost of the forty-five that are under contract at the present time. I have not had any firm offers because I have not yet received the authority of this House to order any more ships, and I will not have such authority until the Supplementary Estimate is approved. But, I firmly believe that I can buy an 8,000 ton ship for $160 a ton, and probably less.
I explained to the House yesterday that for a year and a half to come no ships could be purchased from any of the yards in' the United Kingdom. In answer to the hon. member's question as to a comparison today between the price for a ship built in Canada and a similar ship built in England, the authority being cited of Sir George Hunter that there is only a difference of ten dollars a ton, it may he when I start negotiations with the Canadian yards we may he able to build ships in this country at as low a rate as they are able to in any oi the yards of the United Kingdom. However, I do not want to be too optimistic, and I can assure my hon. friend from Bed Deer (Mr. Clark) that all business men are trained to be most cautious, especially when they have the responsibility of office, such as I have. In respect to whatever further outlays are required on shipbuilding, the money will be expended on a thoroughly conservative and business-like basis.

I think there is one fact that the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) has not taken into consideration in connection with shipments of wheat. It is that the United States have fixed a price for their crop of wheat this year of $2.26 per bushel. There is a great deal of apprehension and concern in Canada to-day, especially in the western part of the Dominion, in regard to the position we shall be in this year with respect to shipping our grain. In regard to those shipments in the past, as
the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) stated, fifty or sixty per cent of our grain has gone through United States ports. There is no doubt in my mind of the necessity of some action on the part of this Government in regard to the fixation of the price of wheat, or in some manner controlling the situation, because I fear our wheat will not be allowed to go through United States ports this year. There will be an embargo placed on it, and the probability of that is greatly strengthened when we take into consideration that the United States will this year have the largest possible crop, according to the estimates made. The last one which I remember reading spoke of there being possibly a surplus of four hundred and fifty million bushels of wheat in the United States this year. When we consider that likelihood there will not be much opportunity for Canada to utilize United States ports for its wheat shipments. Therefore, when the minister states that he is going to take action with respect to a shipbuilding programme which will provide steamships for the Great Lakes and also facilitate the transportation of our wheat this year, I think that action should receive the earnest and hearty support of every member of the House.
Mr. JAMES E. WILSON: While on the subject of wheat transportation, I may say that I read a couple of days ago in a trade paper, a statement by Mr. A. E. Hunter, a member of the Wheat and Flour Millers' Control Commission of the United Kingdom. That gentleman told the National Association of British and Irish Millers that they were now up against a shortage of wheat imports, caused mainly through the diversion to India of a large amount of wheat from Australia, which was intended for the United Kingdom. India has usually exported wheat, but it is now a wheat importing country. As the previous speaker has mentioned, there is great apprehension among the farmers in Western Canada as to the possible profitable marketing of this year's wheat crop. The whole fabric of transportation, international finance, and exchange of commerce throughout the country. particularly with Overseas countries, has broken down as a result of the war, and the carrying on of commerce and transportation therefore becomes a Government undertaking. It is beyond the power oi private individuals to cope .with the situation as efficiently as can be done through Government agencies, and I think the policy which has been inaugurated by the Minister of Marine to develop our shipping

is a splendid one. We are a little late in undertaking it, but it is most necessary and it will be a source of great wealth to Canada to control its own shipping, particularly so now that we have gone into the business of operating railways. These railways can be used to supply the ships, and the ships can be used to a certain extent to furnish the railways with return cargoes, so that I think it is vitally in the interest of Canada to extend our shipbuilding facilities as much as possible. Most business men have been looking forward to the development of a large trade with Overseas countries, but it will not be possible to secure that development without ships. Therefore, I have much pleasure in supporting the programme which has been outlined by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am sorry I overlooked the hon. gentleman's inquiry in reference to the 80,000 tons of steel contracted for in the United States. I am happy to inform him that we do not need to take the balance of the contract unless we desire to. So that disposes of that part

of the hon. member's argument. I thought I made it abundantly clear in Committee yseterday that this country has nothing to fear in shipbuilding competition from our neighbours to the south. I made a very conservative statement yesterday when I said that the ships built by the Emergency Fleet Corporation cost at least $25 a ton more than the 45 ships which the Canadian Government have under construction at the present time. The hon. member talks about building ships at $200 per ton. In the plainest language possible I stated yesterday that our contracts ranged from $180 to $215 a ton. So far as we have gone with our shipbuilding programme, our prices compare favourably with those paid by the United States Government, which has built a vastly greater number of ships than we have contracted for. I have stated over and over again that when it comes to competition with the United Kingdom you cannot get a fixed price there, that everything is on a plus cost basis, as the hon. member has just mentioned. The information I obtained from England is that $150 a ton would be the cost, provided you could get your ships built there now; but it is quite impossible to get any built for a year and a half, and I have given as my authority the well-known shipbuilder, 'Sir George Hunter, of Swan and Hunter. Why the hon. gentleman wants to make it appear that the cost of a Canadian-built ship is so much more than that of a ship built in the United States, and is basing on that supposition his argument that we can get ships built in the United Kingdom at the present time, is more than T am able to follow.

What about the gentleman
|I mentioned who said that contracts were made on the Tyne for ships at $115 a ton? That is not $200 a ton.

House again in Committee on Bill No. 18 respecting Bankruptcy.-Mr. Guthrie.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the Committee last considered this Bill we had reached section 43. Shall section 43 carry?

The hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) who left this afternoon, desired me to ask the Solicitor General to defer consideration of this Bill. He toldj me that a meeting of business men had appointed Mr. La-fleur and Mr. Geoffrion of Montreal to examine the Bill and consult with the Solicitor General about certain points. I told my hon. friend that I would submit his request to the Solicitor General when the Bill came up. He says there are important provisions which they want to discuss, not with the object of blocking the Bill, but in order to make it as faultless as possible.

I saw' the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres at three o'clock to-day and discussed the matter with him. He asked that certain clauses be allowed to stand, to which I agreed, and I assume that before they are considered the representatives of the Quebec Bar will have an opportuhity of discussing them. So I do not quite understand this request.
Yes, I apologize. I did not know that the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) had seen the Solicitor General.

Section agreed to.
On section 45-proof of debts.
Is this the same as the English section?
With one or two modifications, yes.
Will the Solicitor General state briefly the method of proving the debt?

The ordinary method, which has been adopted in the various provinces of Canada, is that of proof by statutory declaration, and that is maintained in this Bill. A debt must be proved by the claimant sending to the trustee through the post, by registered letter, a statutory declaration verifying the debt made before an authorized person. The declaration shall contain a statement of the account, shall specify the vouchers, if any, held by the creditor, and shall state whether the creditor is or is not a secured creditor. That is the prima facie proof that is required.
In the provincial Acts there is a provision by which a person disputing a claim can have it proven in court
That is in this Bill in a subsequent section.

That is a very expensive procedure. A very simply provision, if there is not already one in the Bill, would be that a person filing a claim could, if it was so desired, be brought before the trustee or the judge who has charge of the estate for cross-examination on his account. I do not know that we have any provision of that kind. What I mean is something like the right that now exists of calling upon a man who files an affidavit in court. One can go to a'judge and ask fo.r leave to bring the man before the court for crossexamination. If the provision is simply that the claimant must file an account with a declaration on it, in many cases the declaration is a slipshod thing; very often the . claimant does not make a declaration at all, but gets somebody to sign the paper as if it were sworn to, although it is not sworn to at all. Before the Bill is finally passed, the minister might consider some simple machinery of the kind I have mentioned by which a party could be brought before the trustee, the inspector or preferably the court, and cross-examined on his account. If parties knew that such a system was available, that would have the effect of making people careful as to the kind of account they would file.

Where it is thought by the creditors or the trustee that an account should be disputed, reduced or rejected altogether, proceedings are taken under section 53, but it is not contemplated that a creditor will have to bring an action.
[[DOT]Mr. Guthrie.]
When a claim is disallowed the section provides that:
Such disallowance shall be final and conclusive unless within thirty days after the service or mailing of the said notice or such further time as the court may on application made within thirty days allow, the claimant appeals to the court in accordance with General Rules from the trustee's decision.
It is proposed in these general rules to* arrange procedure for a summary application to the court in order that a claim may be speedily and inexpensively dealt with. Just how that rule will be framed, I am not at present able to state as those rules will require a good deal of consideration. There may be something in the suggestion of my hon. friend that power should be given to the trustee or the creditors to cross-examine the claimant upon his declaration proving his claim. The result of such cross-examination might be that the claim might be rejected or accepted, and further proceedings might be avoided.
I shall be glad to consider the question of an amendment for that purpose.
I do not think it would be wise to have any provision to the effect that a trustee or an inspector should crossexamine a claimant. That matter should be in the hands of the registrar of the court.

The claim does not go to the registrar of the court. The creditor proves his claim to the trustee; the trustee submits it to the creditors, and if they are not satisfied that the claim is a bona fide one, it might be wise to allow them to crossexamine him on the claim at a meeting of creditors.

The creditors have no right to examine a claimant on their own account. That should be the duty of the court. At the present time a claim of that kind is contested, and the trustee becomes the petitioning party to ask that it be disallowed and it is thereupon tested before the court. But to give the creditors the right to cross-examine is not the best method of procedure, nor is it according to the rule which we now have in the court.
My hon. friend does not quite understand the practice that is laid down in this Bill. If a , trustee rejects a claim he serves notice upon the claimant.

What right has the trustee
to reject it?
He may have information that it is not a bona fide claim.
Then he should send it to the court.

The other process is the one adopted in England and in the provinces. Notice is served upon the claimant that the creditors are not satisfied with the claim and the creditor must establish his claim within thirty days after notice is served.
Is the affidavit not prima facie proof that a claim is correct?
That is all it is, prima facie proof. That is the English law, and it has been the Ontario law for thirty years.
It is not the Quebec law. The opposite is the rule. In Quebec the trustee, or curator as he is called, is obliged to contest the claim and the matter is then brought before the court.
He contests it under this section, but merely by serving notice. Then the creditor must proceed.

Section agreed to.
On section 46-proof by secured creditors.

A representative of the Bankers' Association has made a suggestion that another subsection should be added to *this section, to make it clear that a creditor by valuing a security does nothing to release his surety. I do not think under this section there would be any release of a surety, but I see no objection to making the matter clear. The amendment suggested is as subsection 12 in the following words:-
Anything done by a secured creditor in compliance with the provisions of this section shall in no way affect, prejudice or vary any right or remedy such creditor may have against any other person or under any security.

Is not that the ordinary law? Is it not a mistake to put in a clause like this, because it might give ground for the argument that in some other place where the clause is not inserted, the opposite was the effect? I think it is very dangerous to lay down a well known legal principle which follows as a matter of course in a clause of this kind.

I said I would mention
the proposed amendment to the Committee. I quite agree that it is an unnecessary provision.
Amendment negatived.

Section agreed to.
On section 48-postponement of husband's claim:

This clause is somewhat
contentious. Has the minister received a request that it stand for further consideration?
No.

May I request that it be
allowed to stand?

It is not retroactive in
effect, applying only to future transactions. That is the only difference between this and the corresponding section in the English Act.

I understand that the
council of the bar of the province of Quebec desire to discuss this section further with the Solicitor General, as it infringes on the civil law of the province.

On section 50-debts payable at a future
time:

Why do we say six
per cent? Is not the legal rate five per
cent?

I think it would be
well for the sake of uniformity to have five per cent in all Dominion legislation.

speechtext:

The Chairman has made a valuable suggestion. If we say the legal rate, then when the legal rate changes, this will change too.	.
Air. AIcKENZIE:	But in some of the
provinces six per cent is the legal rate, and although this is in a general way Dominion legislation, in its operation it will be provincial. On section 51-priority of claims:

I would suggest that this and the following section stand for further consideration for the reason I gave with respect to section 48.

On section 55-arrest of debtors under certain circumstances:

Paragraph (a) says that if there is reason for believing that the debtor has absconded or is about to abscond " with a view of avoiding payment of the debt in respect of which the bankruptcy petition was filed." Why limit it to the particular, debt in respect of which the bankruptcy petition is filed? A bankruptcy petition may be filed for $200, and the debtor might abscond in order to evade another debt of $5,000.

The provincial law
allows you to arrest a debtor if he is about to abscond. You would have to fall back on that.

The $200 debt would be the only one that was proved. I do not see why it should be limited to the particular debt in respect of which the bankruptcy proceedings are taken. If he owes several debts it is more likely that he will abscond to avoid payment of the largest. I think we should make it read: "With a view of avoiding payment of the debt in respect of which the bankruptcy petition was filed, or any other proved debt."

The creditor of the larger amount might not want the man to be arrested, he might desire to be lenient. There is nothing to deprive any other creditor from taking. proceedings in respect of his debt but we have made this provision to give some particular individual a positive right to do so.
He would not have the right to arrest him unless he absconded for the purpose of evading that particular debt.
Not under this Act.
That might be only one debt out of probably fifteen.	~

You have your own
laws in each province. Under this Act only one creditor is entitled to do it.
, Mr. JACOBS:	There is nothing in the
section to indicate that the trustee would have the right to cause the warrant to issue. Section 55 says:
The court may, by warrant addressed to any constable or prescribed officer of the court, cause a debtor to be arrested.
It does not say whether the trustee would have that right.

The English Act does not limit it and I do not see why we should

be too precise in the matter. The court will act on the application of some party interested. An ordinary stranger could not go to the court; it would have to be either a creditor or a trustee. They are the only two parties I know.

There ought to be some
clearer expression as to the meaning of the word " absconding." Under our system at present in the law of capias it has to be declared in the affidavit that the debtor is -about to leave the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. If it cannot be shown that he is about to leave Quebec and Ontario he could not be capiased. Suppose a man were leaving Quebec to go to Ontario, or Nova Scotia or New Brunswick, would he be considered to be absconding? Or does it mean leaving the Dominion of Canada?

The word "absconding" has a very wide application. Hiding is absconding; so also is keeping house, under the English Act. The word in our Act is "absconding," going from his usual place of residence to some place of retirement unknown to his creditors. "Keeping house" is a term taken from the English Act in section 3, subsection (f): "If he departs from his dwelling house or otherwise absents himself, or begins to keep house." It means leaving his ordinary place of business and secreting or hiding himself.

Suppose a resident of
Montreal did not leave Montreal at all but simply kept in hiding, would he be absconding when he really did not leave his domicile?
If he is in hiding, I think so.

To make it perfectly clear something should be added to this clause. In the jurisdiction in which I practise, absconding means clearing out of the country. As our law of capias comes from the time of the united provinces of Upper and Lower Canada, it means getting out of Quebec and Ontario. It would be wise and would avoid any possibility of useless litigation if the clause were made somewhat clearer in regard to the meaning of "absconding."
Would you say, absents himself from Canada, or from any particular province?
As this is a federal Act I should think "absconding" would mean leaving the Dominion.
If we say, absconding from the province in which he carries on his business that would be satisfactory.

Departs out of the
province, or being out of the province remains out of it?
Yes, out of the province in which he had his domicile or carried on his business.
That would not do, because it is not wrong for a man to depart from the province.
That is qualified by the words immediately following: "with a view of avoiding payment," etc.

Suppose a man owes 810,000 in debts and is insolvent and a creditor for $300 presents his petition, and the man skips out, not with a view to avoiding payment of the $300, but to get clear of the $9,700, and the only man that can prosecute him is the $300 creditor. That creditor might come to an arrangement with the debtor and say, "If you do not pay me I will prosecute you, and I am the only man that can
5 p.m. prosecute you." It seems to me that the provision is either good or bad, and it should be as good for one as for the other. I would suggest that there be added the words "or any proved debt."
Is that clause similar to the clause in the English Act?

Yes, our section is drawn from the section in the English Act. The English law has been in force so long that every section has been judicially interpreted and if we start changing the wording we change the meaning of the authority. It has been so carefully reviewed, amended and interpreted that it would be wise for us to take the benefit of their experience rather than make changes. Unless there is some good reason for a change I would rather not make it,

I notice the reference'at the end of section 55 says:
(Part Eng. Sec. 23 modified.)
What part of that has been modified?

We have inserted here a provision about assignment that we have not in the English Act. Subsection (a) of the Act reads:

A few days ago we passed a Bill which subjects a woman to two years in the penitentiary if she happens to. put too big a fire in her stove and her house is burned down; that is No. 1. I think yesterday the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce, in his innocence and good nature, introduced a Bill imposing fine and imprisonment upon a person who happens to sell one of brother Loggie's lobster cans supposed to contain a pound of food, whereas in fact it may only contain fourteen ounces; that is No. 2. And the Solicitor General, not to be outdone in this criminal business, introduces this clause, whereby if a man institutes civil proceedings against a debtor, which he has a perfect right to do, without first examining himself-as it is presumed every one does before taking such a step,-he is subject to the fines and penalties prescribed. Why should we be doing these things? This is a free country and every man is presumed to be honest until the contrary is proved. There is no necessity for these innovations, and I must protest with all the energy that is in me against creating these criminal possibilities. I am not going to say anything further, I leave the entire responsibility not only upon the Solicitor General, but upon the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend, as usual, has very greatly exaggerated the facts. It is nothing unusual to have penal clauses in a Bill. During every session we pass Bills in which provision is made for fine and imprisonment for violations of the law, and my hon. friend could make pre-

cisely the same argument against those measures. What is the result of all such legislation? Are there cases of men languishing for weeks and months in jail? My hon. friend knows that nothing of the kind happens. In the first place, before a man can be consigned to jail and suffer in the manner my hon. friend has indicated, he is brought before a magistrate and there is a preliminary hearing. That in itself is a safeguard. If he elects to be tried by a jury ait the next court of competent jurisdiction, he is able to obtain bail. My hon. friend has magnified the effect of criminal provisions in statutory enactments. I have not taken much interest in this Bill, but I happened to be in the House a little before six o'clock and I heard him putting forward an argument which on the face of it seems plausible. He says that there is no [DOT] penalty under the Criminal Code for malicious laying of an information under that Code. That is true, I think. But, I submit, there is a real difference between the case of a malicious prosecution for an offence under the Criminal Code or common law, and malicious laying of an information under this Bankruptcy Bill. It would seldom happen that a man's business interest would be advantaged by laying an information under the Criminal Code for any offence contained therein. One could hardly imagine a retail dealer seeking to ruin a rival by laying an information against him maliciously for, let us say, theft. But in this case where a 'trader would have an interest in ruining a rival-and many cases of that kind occur *almost daily-I can imagine his taking *advantage of this law very successfully from his own standpoint.
The leader of the Opposition has dwelt upon the fact that a judge of the high court must give judgment upon the petition. But the damage is done before the judge gives his decision. The mere filing of a petition in bankruptcy against a solvent trader is ruinous to that man's credit, and that is the reason why some 25,000 small retail dealers throughout Canada desire, as I understand it, to be safeguarded under this Bill. In other words, a man may have a direct, immediate business interest in filing a petition in bankruptcy against a rival trader. In Toronto, I have frequently been in the civil courts as a spectator, and I have seen numerous cases of business disputes in which action had been taken, founded upon the most obviously malicious motives and declared by the judge to be so. If any one fSlr Thomas White.!
doubts me, let him go to a division court where the smaller cases are tried and where traders of a certain type sue and are sued, and he will realize the danger there is in allowing a small, irresponsible and malicious trader to file a petition in bankruptcy against a rival. What remedy has his rival in the civil courts? The leader of the Opposition says that for malicious prosecution there is the remedy in tort at common law, a civil remedy, for which the only penalty is damages. Let us take the case of a trader who is bailiff-proof and who determines to ruin a rival. He acquires a claim against his rival, or he has a straw man take an assignment of a claim and file a petition in bankruptcy against the man against whom his animosity and cupidity are directed. The petition is filed, and that man's credit is gone. He may be ruined if it proceeds no further; even if the judge, before whom the matter comes, decides in favour of the party against whom the proceedings are taken, the man's credit is gone.
My hon. friend has stated that the Government has been very free this year with legislation applying the criminal law. Does he realize what we are doing in this Bill? As regards the present situation, which we have had for many years in Canada and , under which men have traded here, we have no provision whereby men may be thrown into bankruptcy under a proceeding such as is provided for by this Bill. This Bill changes all that; it provides that any creditor, no matter what his motives may be, may file a petition, the effect of which may be to ruin some solvent trader, because a man may be solvent although trading on a very small margin. Without some safeguard to such trader, there is nothing the Government has brought down this session more objectionable than this Bill if, as is the attitude of my hon. friend, it leaves traders without any safeguard against proceedings which may be taken by malicious creditors. That is the distinction between this case and the case put forward by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster),-that for malicious prosecution under the Criminal Code there is only civil remedy. It is almost impossible to imagine a case in which there is the direct element of personal advantage in laying a charge of theft. Not only that, a charge of theft has to be established by much stronger, much more clear, cogent and convincing evidence than the argument by which a man would seek to justify a petition in bankruptcy. Up to date, it has not been brought to my attention, although it may have happened,

that a business trader seeking to outrival a competitor has searched the Criminal Code to find upon what offence he can most conveniently lay an information against his rival. But this places the machinery right in his hand, and I have read of dozens of cases in the reports of division court hearings in Toronto where the element of malice was- undoubtedly present for the purpose of injuring a trade rival. This machinery would be at once available in such a case. The remedy in damages cannot be adequate because the man who brings the proceedings or causes them to be brought may be in a position, so far as civil proceedings are concerned, to snap his fingers at a prosecutor, and yet as soon as he has filed the petition, he has practically ruined his competitor. If we are bringing into this House legislation that changes the situation under which business has been carried on in Canada for many years, it is incumbent upon the House to the utmost of its power to protect from abuse of proceedings under that measure those who are to be subjected to its provisions. I have not had an opportunity of listening to previous discussions on this Bill; but, listening to the arguments put forward here this afternoon, though feeling that I am not in many ways as competent to pronounce upon the merits of the provision as many who have spoken, I believe the House should lean towards protecting that man against whom proceedings may be taken under this measure.

speechtext: What is the application of the reference to ex post facto criminal law?
