speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why, then, are these retail men so desirous of being safeguarded against this very thing?

Because they have some unfounded suspicion about something they had never any occasion to be afraid of. There has never been such a law in this country since 1875. I do not remember the days of 1875 and the few years before that during which the old Act was in force, but I challenge my hon. friend to produce a single case where anybody maliciously laid an information under that Act or took proceedings against his neighbour to ruin hipi. I never heard of such a thing.
I base my argument entirely upon this fact: When we made pur Criminal Code in 1892 we simply took the English law as it then stood, and our own Statutes; we were

perfectly satisfied with the English criminal law as we found it. and with the judicial interpretations by the courts of Great Britain. Here we are not taking the English law, but are adding new provisions to it, creating a condition that will put in the hands of one person the power of putting his neighbour in jail, without any justification whatever, and keeping him there indefinitely when there may be no more malice in his heart than there is in the heart of the Acting Prime Minister. We are putting this power in the hands of somebody who may or may not use it. Would it not be time enough to provide such a law when a case of this kind arises? I promise the Acting Prime Minister and the Solicitor General that if advantage is taken of this Act to do anything improper within three or six months after it passes this House, I shall hasten to their side to pass legislation preventing any such thing. But I am not in favour of putting unnecessary criminal laws on the statute book under which a man may, without any justification, send his neighbour to jail while his children are left to suffer cold and hunger. But the responsibility is not mine, the responsibility rests with the Government, more particularly as I have presented my views and, I think, those of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House.

I would not impose on the time of the Committee had not the Acting Prime Minister directed some of his remarks to answering an argument I had brought forward. His argument was this: We are introducing new legislation, unusual legislation; this unusual legislation is open to the possibility of abuse; in order to discourage the possibility of abuse, we are going to make it a penal offence to abuse the Act.
First of all, let me say that the province of Quebec has had laws upon its statute book for many decades past, whereby any creditor who had a claim of $200 against a man who had generally stopped making payments, could file what amounted to a petition of bankruptcy against him; that is, he could make what we call a demand of abandonment, which would be supported by affidavit and then filed in court. This is a very summary way of bringing a man into insolvency and forcing him to distribute his property among his creditors.
I have not been practicing for a great number of years, but I have never in the course of my experience known of an action instituted by a man who had been put into insolvency by a competitor in which the

insolvent claimed that his competitor had wilfully and maliciously used the machinery of the law for the purpose-of damaging him. Therefore, I think the Government in placing this section 97 on the statute book are trying to guard against something which is not likely to happen. It has not happened, as far as my experience goes, in a province in which for a generation and a half, creditors have had the powers which are given under this Bill.
The second argument of the Acting Prime Minister was this: He first of all said: I admit that generally the abuse of legal process of a criminal nature is guarded against merely by the right of the injured innocent party to take an action in damages either for false arrest or for the laying of false information against him; but, he added, under this Act, there will be greater opportunities given to a man in commercial life to do something wrongful against his neighbour. I do not agree with my hon. friend. Take this case for instance: An information is laid against a high-class solicitor for embezzling the funds of his clients. Now that would enormously hurt the solicitor, even if the charge were dismissed. Or again, suppose a false and malicious accusation is made against a man occupying a high professional position, or a respectable merchant, charging him with some hideous crime. His reputation may be. hurt, his business may be damaged, and financial loss may be sustained just the same as in a case of malicious proceedings under this Bankruptcy Act in regard to an ordinary merchant. That being so, why put upon the statute book this ususual provision. Why has the English law given to the wronged party merely an action in damages in all these cases? There is some good reason, and it is this, that the policy of the law has not been to frighten the innocent and legitimate complainant. It is often difficult enough for a complainant who has a perfectly justified complaint against a fellow citizen to urge that complaint before the court; the tradition of the British law has been that the courts are open to him, and if he uses them maliciously he is liable in damages. I believe that our laws should proceed on 'broad general principles 'and that we should have as few exceptions as possible. For these reasons I believe that this legislation is unsound and unnecessary. It is difficult for me, having glanced at section 4 of the Act, to see how a malicious institution of proceedings can take place. The man who has a claim against a debtor is not- able

to put that debtor into bankruptcy before he goes before a court and justifies that claim as a proper and well-founded one. On the whole I believe that this proposed legislation is both unnecessary and undesirable.

At the last sitting of the Committee when this proposal of the member for London (Mr. Cronyn) was submitted I asked that it should stand over until I had time to consider it. In the meantime I have taken the resolution up with the officials of the department and they are inclined to the view that if it were adopted it would give rise to a good deal of trouble and difficulty. Therefore, unless the hon. gentleman is anxious to press his amendment, I would suggest that he withdraw it.

I have no special desire to press the amendment at this session. It was perhaps too drastic a step to take now involving as it does so marked a change in what has been the accepted policy of the country ever since the question of immigration was first considered. I shall therefore ask leave of the Committee to withdraw the resolution.
Might I, before resuming my seat, express the hope that after due reflection the department may see fit at another session to adopt some plan whereby we may escape the ungracious and delicate duty of refusing admission to our country to some particular race or nation. Something has been said of contemplated legislation by the United States which will greatly restrict, if it does not wholly prohibit, immigration into that country for a period of years. At least two Bills proposing such action were introduced at the last sitting of Congress and were referred to the Select Standing Committee of the House of Kepresentatives on Immigration and Colonization. Those hon. members who have read the evidence adduced before that Committee^ and the report presented on the 29th of January last to the House of Kepresentatives, cannot fail to be struck by the strong and wide-spread opinion which exists throughout the United States in favour of some such measure. If I may be permitted I should like to read a part of the final clause of the report of the majority of that Committee expressing their view of this matter:
The far-famed melting pot has proven to a great degree a delusion and a snare. We feel that it is now time that we were beginning to look after those of our own household, rather than to open our ports to many who know nothing of our laws, our customs, our standards of living, and never intend to learn of them.
It is true there was also a minority report presented to the House by two members thereof, Kepresentatives A. J. Sabath, of Illinois, and Isaac Siegel, of New York. The minority report, as was only natural, dwelt with pride upon the record on the field of battle of many who had-been immigrants, or the descendants of immigrants, but despite the eloquent character of that minority report, a general opinion prevailed that the House would have passed a Bill to further restrict immigration had the opportunity been afforded. It is a matter of record, however, and is known doubtless to many of the members of this House, that there was an almost continuous filibuster maintained during the session, and these Bills, with many others, fell by the wayside as unfinished business. Now, if the United States does, in the immediate future, pass any such law-and undoubtedly the attempt will be made at the next session of Congress -it will result in increasing pressure on Canada by immigrants from the southeastern part of Europe to obtain entry to this country. It therefore seems to me to be the duty of this House to safeguard our country in such way as we can to prevent too great a flood of those who may not prove best fitted to become future citizens.
I have to confess to a want of faith in the efficacy of section 13 of this Bill, to which the minister has made reference. It is an extension, and, perhaps, a wise extension, of the powers contained in section 38 of the old Act, and undoubtedly under those powers the Government of the day could exclude any person, any race, any nationality. But le,t us assume for a moment-a violent assumption perhaps-that this Government goes out of power and that a Government of the ordinary type which formerly administered the affairs of Canada is in control. If the then Minister of Immigration undertook, under the powers conferred by this section, to bar the people of some particular nation from entering into Canada, imagine what would result. In the first place we would have all the families in Canada from that nation protesting against the refusal to allow their relatives to join them. Indeed, we would have every member of that interdicted nation in Canada making common cause against the ruling; because it is a striking feature of the immigration movement that a successful immigrant is the keenest person to have his fellow-countryman, whether related or not, share in his good fortune. It is an exceedingly difficult matter to persuade him that too free a movement of this kind may

eventually result in damage to himself and others. In the second place, if the proposed immigrants were a good type of untrained labour you would have the large employers of the country protesting, and they would bring weighty arguments against the enforcement of an Order in Council calling for exclusion. A few nights ago I had a short talk with one of the largest employers of this class of labour in Canada. We were discussing one of the nations in Southeastern Europe-I prefer not to be more definite in that regard-when he said quite frankly: "Yes, they are excellent workmen, they are vigorous, they are untiring, but you will never make citizens of them. In truth, their ideal is against such a destiny; they are at best but temporary sojourners in this country."
Added to the pressure from immigrants and employers, you would have, of course, great clamour from steamship and transportation companies, and labour agencies. I do not believe any Government would withstand the pressure thus brought to bear. We would then be back again in exactly the position in which we have always been, and suibject perhaps to a flood of less desirable people, a flood which, by its very volume, would divert the lesser currents from Northern Europe, the record of whose people, as I have tried to point out, is that they become tillers of our soil and assimilate with the present population.
Some comment has been made as to the purport of the proposed amendment, the suggestion being made that it was aimed to exclude certain nationalities or religions. As one witty member of the press gallery remarked, I was apparently trying to exclude the Pope and include the Kaiser. I do not think I need assure the House that no such idea entered my head. As I explained, the lines suggested were rough-and-ready boundaries, not intended to be accepted as final; indeed they were only used to try to illustrate the principles that I was endeavouring to bring before the House. These principles were based on the results disclosed by official records. If those records can be attacked-and they have not as yet been assailed-much of my argument would go for naught. The restrictions suggested are thus founded on what is known of certain ethnic and sociological characteristics, largely due to racial origin and climatic conditions and indelibly fixed during the course of many centuries.
Perhaps I owe a word of apology to the Committee for again occupying its atten-

tion. As was natural, hon. members from Western Canada were more particularly interested in this question, and they were able to bring to the problem the great value of their personal experience. I come from old Ontario where, although there are many thousands of acres ready for intensive cultivation, we could not expect to get any large proportion of new immigration. As a matter of fact, I approached the problem with a feeling that nothing should be done to bar any immigrant. All reasons, financial and otherwise, pointed that way. It was only after making such study as I could of what had happened in the neighbouring Republic, and to a lesser extent in our own country, that I came to the conclusion that we should take a very strong stand, for a time at any rate, against allowing too free an entry.
Perhaps some explanation of the interest I have in this subject is due to the fact that for the past twelve years it has been my duty and my privilege to make an annual visit to the Western Provinces, and the result of those trips has been to confirm my optimistic belief in our country; in fact, to raise it almost to a state of religious fervour. Do I need, then, any excuse for striving to the poor best of my ability to so shape the future of our race in this one particular that it may prove worthy of a great heritage?

I am certainly in favour of the very best class of immigrants we can get. But can we very logically compare ourselves to-day with the United States? We have the same area of habitable land, but while they have 120,000,000 of people we have scarcely 8,000,000. Does the hon. member (Mr. Cronyn) think that we are in a position to apply the 'same rigid laws to immigration as the United States are applying, situated as they are?

I think, Mr. Chairman,, financially, and, perhaps, from the point of view of the need of population, we are hardly in a position to do so. If we did apply as rigid rules as I suggest it would undoubtedly delay the material progress of the country. But I think there is something greater than mere material progress, and I am one of those who fear the United States may have built up its wonderful prosperity at the risk of the future wellbeing of the race. We are not yet able to judge what the result of the " melting pot " will be. I suppose there is none living to-day who will ^ee the full fruition of the policy adopted by that country. I would

rather that >we bent our backs further and sweated more freely in the . effort to carry our present burden than imperil what future generations should inherit.
Amendment (Mr. Cronyn) withdrawn.

If the minister wishes [DOT]to say to an immigrant that he may bring in his arms, his gun or his musket or his rifle, it would be better to state! so, because guns are now made that can be taken apart into pieces not more than a foot in length, and if one wants to conceal them on one's person he can do so; and so a thing that is not intended to be made a crime might be made a crime under this Bill. 1 suppose it is no offence for a man to bring a gun into this country, but the moment he tries to conceal it under his coat he becomes a criminal.
Amendment agreed to.

I'move to insert as a new section after section 14 of the present Bill the following:.
14. (A) Section forty-one of the said Act is repealed and the following is substituted therefor :

"41. Whenever any person other than a Canadian citizen advocates in Canada the overthrow by force or violence of the government of Great Britain or Canada, or other British dominion, colony, possession or dependency, or the overthrow by force or violence of constituted law and authority, or the assassination of any official of the Government of Great Britain or Canada or other British dominion, colony, possession or dependency, or of any foreign government, or advocates or teaches the unlawful destruction of property, or shall by word or act create or attempt to create riot or public disorder in Canada, or shall by common repute belong to Or be suspected of belonging to any secret society or organization which extorts money from, or in any way attempts to control any resident of Canada by force or threat of bodily harm, or by blackmail, or who is a member of or affiliated with any organization extertaining or teaching disbelief in or opposition to organized government; such person for the purposes of this Act shall be considered as belonging to the prohibited or undesirable classes, and shall be liable to deportation, and it shall be the duty of any officer becoming cognizant thereof, and the duty of the clerk, secretary or other official of any municipality in Canada wherein such person may be, to forthwith send a written complaint thereof to the minister giving full particulars."
This section is practically the same as the section in the old law, with this exception, that we have included in the prohibited

class, such persons as those who advocate the overthrow of government by force or violence and the unlawful destruction of property. We have amended this section merely to bring it into conformity with the other section in the Bill.
Mr. .1ACOBS: I should like to have some information from the minister with respect to this passage in the section:
Or sQial] by common repute belong to or be suspected of belonging to any secret society or organization which extorts money from, or in any way attempts to control any resident of Canada by force or threat of bodily harm, or by blackmail.

That is part of the old law. I understand that there were in Canada some years ago certain societies constituted of foreign-born people who carried on a good deal of work of that kind, and the department at that time found it necessary to put this provision in the Bill. I think one of them was a Chinese society called the "Black Hand Society" which operated in that direction.

The section says further
that among those prohibited from coming into Canada are those who are members of or affiliated with "any organization entertaining or teaching disbelief in or opposition to organized government." We know that Great Britain has been a harbour of refuge to all classes of people who teach all kinds of political beliefs. They knew they would have sanctuary in England, and were always permitted by law to come there. As I understand it, Scotland Yard and other institutions of that kind were able to keep proper tab on them by knowing just where they were to be found in England. If I remember aright, the famous Russian nihilist, Stepniak and several of his followers lived in England for many years and taught their doctrines with more or less success, always under the protection of the British authorities. If we adopt this section, we shall be restricting the right of residence in this country to a greater degree than is done in England, which surely ought to be the country that wre should follow in matters of this knid.
I am not so sure, but that on account of conditions that have existed during the last year or two, we shall find the English Government changing its law in this regard. 1
By Order in Council, and only for the period of the war.

I am not so certain of that; I think we shall find some very strin-

gent provisions placed by the British Parliament before very long. The question is whether or not we should permit to enter Canada or to remain in Canada people who openly and violently advocate the overthrow of constitutional government as we understand it. This suggests that we should not do so, and I think we should have a provision of this kind in our law.

Might I point out this
instance to the minister? The Bolshevist Government is the de facto Government in Russia to-day, and for various reasons, which I need not relate to the Committee, the Bolshevist Government is not very popular in this country and in some other countries. Supposing a society was formed for the purpose of overthrowing, by violence, the Government of Messrs. Lenine and Trotsky, do I understand that any person who advocates a view of that kind would be prohibited from entering Canada or if here would he be ordered to be deported from this country?

I think the hon. member would have to take the whole section. The first part of the section reads:
Whenever any person other than a Canadian citizen advocates in Canada the overthrow by force or violence of the Government of Great Britain or Canada, or other British Dominion,, coloncy, possession or dependency or the overthrow by force or violence of constituted law and authority.
I would think that would be in Canada. We are not particularly concerned with what the people do, say in the heart of Russia.
I am referring to Canada. If any person in Canada advocates the overthrow of the Bolshevik Government, what would happen?

I doubt very much if that person would come within the scope of this section, and it is not intended that he should. It is intended to cover only those who would advocate the violent overthrow of constituted Government in this country.

I think the clause says
otherwise :
Or the overthrow by force or violence of constituted law and authority, or the assassination of any official of the Government of Great Britain or Canada or other British Dominion, colony, possession or dependency, or of any foreign Government.
That is the part I object to.

It is taken from the old Act. the corresponding section of which reads:-

Whenever any person other than a Canadian citizen advocates in Canada the overthrow toy force or violence of the Government ot Great Britain or Canada or other British dominion, colony, possession or dependency, or the overthrow toy force or violence of constituted law and authority, or the assassination of any official of the Government of Great Britain or Canada or other British dominion, colony, possession or dependency or of any foreign government-*
The draftsman has simply included the provisions of the old law. I cannot see any very great necessity for retaining the words " or of any foreign government."

No. I think that ought to be struck out. We should not forget Tennyson's words that England is a land " where girt by friend or foe a man may speak the thing he will." He ought to be satisfied if we safeguard the British Empire. Foreign governments ought to look after themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend's quotation was a very happy one with regard to England. It is quite understandable that England can afford to be fairly lax and fairly generous in regard to the shelter of any particular class of people even if they go to violent extremes in speech, for the reason that the British are a homogeneous people and the foreign born are not in sufficient numbers to constitute any real danger to the state. But the situation in this country, especially in Western Canada, is fundamentally different. We have immense numbers of foreigners here who are easily misled, and it is quite manifest that the doctrines of those who openly preach sedition and advocate the overthrow of organized governments by force exercise a much more dangerous influence in an atmosphere such as ours than they would in England. Therefore, I think that the first part of the section is absolutely necessary. With regard to the other part, my hon. friend asked whether it would apply to a man, for instance, who advocated the overthrow of the Lenine and Trotsky government-whether he would be allowed to come into this country. I read all through the section the words "constituted government" and I maintain, and I think my hon. friend will be compelled to agree with me, that the Lenine and Trotsky Government is not a constituted government because they obtained power by refusing to let the constituent assembly meet, and took the country by force.
That is the way most governments obtain power.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Not by force of arms- brute force-but by moral force. In this case the constituent assembly was on the point -of meeting, but Lenine and Trotsky absolutely refused to let it meet, and they seized power by force of arms. I would not regard that aS a constitutional form of government.
It is the de facto government.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: De facto by sheer force of arms, but certainly not de jure.
Does my hon. friend consider that Oliver Cromwell's government was a constitutional government, when Cromwell seized power?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Whatever opinions I
may hold in regard to Oliver Cromwell- and I cherish pretty strong ones-I think he is a long way ahead of Lenine and Trotsky.
As regards the manner in which he seized power, his case was on all fours with Lenine and Trotsky's.

The suggestion of my
hon. friend, as I understand it, is this: That we should not pay any attention to any person who in this country advocates the assassination of an official in South America, let us say. I am quite willing to leave it to the judgment of the Committee whether we should allow such a man to remain in Canada or not.

I think the minister did not quite understand what my hon. friend intended to convey. His idea, as I understood it, was that there might be some persons living in Canada, inhabitants, say, of a South American republic, who had been displaced from power perhaps by a revolution and, while in Canada, were plotting a counter-revolution to regain power.

My hon. friend will pardon me. The section explains itself. It reads: "Whenever any person other than a Canadian citizen advocates in Canada. .	.
the assassination of any official of the Government of Great Britain or Canada. . . or of any foreign Government." That is, any person- in Canada shall be liable to deportation who advocates the assassination of any official of any foreign Government.

Perhaps I might give the Secretary of State another instance: One of our Allies, King Peter of Serbia, obtained power by the murder of his predecessor,

King Alexander. I have no doubt that if King Peter came to Canada he would be received in the way in which all high dignitaries are received here.
New section as proposed agreed to.
On the motion of Mr. Calder, the Committee reverted to the consideration of section 2-domicile:

I beg to move that clause 2 be amended by inserting the following proviso after paragraph (1):
Provided further that no person who belongs to the prohibited or undesirable classes within the meaning of section forty-one of this Act shall be capable of acquiring Canadian domicile.
The effect of the amendment will be briefly this: The persons we have just been speaking of, who advocate the destruction of property and the violent overthrow of constitutional governments, if they are not Canadian citizens, will not be allowed to acquire Canadian domicile so far as our right to deport them is concerned. Under the law as it now stands, once a man lives in Canada for a period of five years and acquires a domicile, whether or not he becomes a Canadian citizen, he cannot be deported.
The effect of this will be that as regards this class they shall be deportable whenever they are found, so long as they have not become Canadian citizens. If they became Canadian citizens in the ordinary way by naturalization, the only way they could be got at afterwards would be under the Criminal Code.
Bill as amended reported.

On motion of Hon. A. K. Maclean (Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce) Bill No. 74, to amend the Fertilizers Act, 1909, was read the second time and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On Section 1, subsection (c)-fertilizer.

I move that the words " or lime, as carbonate, hydrate or oxide be struck out. It has been represented by those who manufacture lime for treatment of the soil that this amendment should be made on the ground that lime is not a fertilizer, and the technical officers of the department so instruct me.

How does the minister class slag?

Mr. A>
K. MACLEAN: Slag contains fertilizing ingredients while lime does not. Lime is used for treating certain soils, such as acid soil and what is termed " sour " land, but it furnishes no fertilizing ingredients to the soil. Slag, of course, contains phosphorous which is released and enriches the soil.
Is it intended that slag shall be subject to inspection and analysis under this Act?

Yes. I have some further amendments to offer. In the last line of subsection (c) I move to insert after the word " ordinary " the word " untreated," so that it will read "ordinary untreated stable manure."

I think thiis Act is hardly applicable to fertilizer like slag, which is not put up in factories but is carried in shiploads and in large quantities in carloads to various parts of the country. This Bill provides that every package of manure shall be subject to a stamp tax. I do not see how it can apply to material that is sold in the way slag is sold.

Slag is a fertilizer. The purchasing public must have some protection and must be assured that the slag is worth purchasing, and it is not within the power of the ordinary consumer of fertilizer to ascertain for himself whether certain slag contains fertilizing ingredients. It must be inspected. In this Bill, while it is provided that a label must be attached, it is also provided that when the fertilizer is sold in bulk the
10 p.m. information which would ordinarily be attached to the label shall be given in the invoice.
Mr. .7. E. SINCLAIR: Will the definition given here of fertilizer include such fertilizers as mussel mud and shell mud, which are both used largely in eastern Canada?
No.
The clause, as I read it, seems to indicate that it would.

Will it include sea manure
and kelp? A good deal of -that is used in my county for manure, and it would be very cumbrous and inconvenient to have to put stamps on an ox load of sea manure or kelp going from the seashore to the farm.

Fish offal and
lobster shells are other material commonly used for manure.

It will be found that this can only refer to fertilizer which is manufactured. If natural manure were sold in any form it would not be manufactured and the requirements of the Act would not apply. I think the section should remain as it is because the purpose of the Act is to protect the consumer or the producer. If a dealer presumes to sell fertilizer in the ordinary way it would be necessary to have it examined or inspected so that the public would know what they were getting. Kelp or any natural fertilizer might be very easily imitated and the public should be protected.

Would it riot be absurd to have an analyst inspect kelp, or lobster shells which were being sold by some person to a neighbour to put on his land? The difficulty does not come in there. It has reference to the manufactured manures. It does not apply to these natural manures like mussel mud, lobster shells, fish offal and various other things that are used by the farmers. Fraud takes place where manures are manufactured.
As a matter of fact these things are not sold.
They are sometimes.

I know of a number of cases where men who own ox teams go to the shore, load up with kelp or sea manure, and sell it to poor widows. It would be a foolish thing to stop a man half way to his destination and weigh his load. I think the insertion of the word "manufactured" would cover it.
I do not differ from hon. gentlemen opposite but I want the section to be effective. The suggestion made is really unnecessary as the commodities to which they refer are not dealt in.
Why not strike out the word "natural" and substitute the word "m anuf actured" ?
I would rather insert after the word "natural" the word "manufactured."
How could you have, a natural manufactured manure?
It might be very easily manufactured by the application of some chemical. The process of manufacture might be so slight that it would hardly be recognized.

I agree with the .minister in regard to the need of the inspection of fertilizers to protect the farmers and consumers. But in this definition of fertilizer you would include mussel mud which is a natural fertilizer and we have many people in Prince Edward Island who take it out of rivers and sell it to farmers in lots of from a ton to a carload. Unless the word "manufactured" were inserted it would include all fertilizers ol this kind. While it may be necessary to have manufactured fertilizers inspected to see if they are up to the standard, it is going very far to say that this sea manure shall be made subject to the provisions of this Act. It contains all the ingredients, phosphoric acid, nitrogen and potash, and if you have to put a stamp on every hundred pounds sold by the vendor to the consumer it would be simply ridiculous. 1 would like the minister to consider that point.
I would suggest that the word "natural" be struck out and the word "manufactured" substituted.

If you struck out the word " natural," that would be sufficient in itself, because the word "artificial" implies manufacture. I would therefore move that the words "natural or" be struck out; that the words " or lime as carbonate, hydrate or oxide" in the seventeenth line be struck out, and that there be inserted, after the word "ordinary" in the eighteenth line, the word " untreated." The paragraph will now read:
(c) "fertilizer" includes every artificial manure containing phosphoric acid or nitrogen or potash, except ordinary, untreated, stable manure.
Now that you are going to cut out the words "natural or" in the fifteenth line, to make the paragraph read correctly, you will have to cut out the words "except ordinary untreated stable manure."
If treated it becomes artificial.
Cut that out altogether.

Yes, that is correct. I beg to move:
That the words "except ordinary stable manure" be struck out.
The clause will now read:
The word "fertilizer" includes every artificial manure containing phosphoric acid or nitrogen or potash.
Paragraph as amended, agreed to.

On paragraph (d)-guaranteed analysis:

I move:
That paragraph (d) be amended by striking out the word " nitrogen " at the end of the twenty-first line and inserting the words "ammonia and"; also by striking out the words "and lime."
The paragraph will then read:
-must be stated in terms of phosphoric acid, ammonia and potash.
Why is "nitrogen" removed ?
"Ammonia" is a better known term.
Is not nitrogen an important ingredient?
You do not mean to say that ammonia and nitrogen are similar?
It is the same thing, and to speak of ammonia is another way of speaking of nitrogen.
It is a long time since I studied chemistry, but what the minister says has' a strange sound in my ears.

I am giving the hon. gentleman the information the officer gives me.
Paragraph as amended, agreed to.

I wish to add as subsection (h) a definition of the word "available:"
"Available" as applied to the phosphoric acid,
[DOT] the ammonia, or the potash stated in the guaranteed analysis, means that quantum of the total phosphoric acid, or ammonia, or potash present which is available for plant use within one year of its application to the soil.
Would not the word "content" be better than the word "present" in the second to last line?

I think the word "present" is the one ordinarily used. You may have a great deal of phosphoric acid in a fertilizer which would not be released for a long time, consequently the fertilizer would have no immediate value. The value of the fertilizer largely depends upon the rapidity with which the fertilizing ingredients are released, and it was considered desirable to have this definition.

Is it not very difficult to tell the time within which the ingredients, or the fertilizing properties, of any manure will be communicated to the soil? Do not the release of the fertilizing ingredients depend largely upon weather conditions- the amount of moisture, and so on?
It has to be determined by experiments conducted by scientific men.

I notice that in the next clause the word "content" is used. Does that mean the same thing as "present" in the clause under consideration? If it does it is always wiser, as matter of drafting to employ the same terms.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 2-How phosphoric acid contents to be stated.

I propose to amend this section and I have sent to hon. gentlemen opposite two copies of the contemplated amendment. Since the first reading of this Bill the officers of the department have been in communication with the manufacturers of fertilizer and the representatives of farmers, and they have gone over the different clauses. I move that section 2A of the present Bill be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
Every person before selling: or offering for sale in Canada any fertilizer, shall either mark upon each package of fertilizer, the following particulars, or attach a label to each such package containing such particulars, or when the fertilizer is sold in bulk shall set out such particulars on the invoice, namely :-
1.	Brand name and trade mark, if any.
2.	Registration number.
3.	Guaranteed analysis, stating separately:
Minimum percentage only.
(a)	The percentage of ammonia.
(b)	The percentage of available phosphoric
acid and the total phosphoric acid.
(c)	The percentage of potash soluble in
water.
4.	The name and address of the manufacturer or seller.
In the case of bone meal, tankage or other organic products, and basic slag, the phosphoric acid shall be stated as total phosphoric acid also. When leather in any form, wool, waste, hair, or any inert organic nitrogenous material, forms part of any fertilizer, the percentage of such ingredients must be mentioned in the guaranteed analysis, unless by processing the nitrogen has been made available in such materials. When potash is derived from sulphate of potash or carbonate of potash it may be so stated in the guaranteed analysis.

Where will the manufacturer
obtain the registered number?
From the department.

Every time he has a new
brand he must send it to Ottawa to have it registered?

Yes. I should
like to have the assistance of the Committee in suitably wording this amend-

ment. For instance, I am not too well satisfied with the wording of the first part:
Every person before selling or offering for sale in Canada any fertilizer-
-shall do so and so. In many places fertilizer is frequently sold, .particularly to owners of gardens, in very small packages. It is not intended that the Bill shall apply to such sales, and possibly there might in the present wording of the amendment be some limitation.

Should not the word " manufactured '' be inserted in the second line after the word "any." That is to say:
Every person before selling or offering for sale in Canada any manufactured fertilizer-
*and so on.
, Mr. A. K. MACLEAN:	Fertilizer is already properly defined.

In sub-paragraph 4 of the amendment the expression " manufacturer or seller " occurs. Does " seller " have the same meaning as " agent," which is referred to in paragraph (a) of section 1, or has it the same meaning as the word " vendor " in section 9?
I move to substitute the word " agent " for the word " seller " in sub-paragraph 4 of the amendment.

It seems to me that
the word " agent " hardly connotes the idea that is intended to be conveyed. I would imagine that there are a number of merchants who deal in fertilizers but who are not agents for any special manufacturer. Is it 'the intention to call all such merchants agents ?
The word "agent" there really has a definition in this Act.
I know. That is just what I am finding fault with, if I may do so without disrespect.
That is so.

It does seem to me a great mistake to give to a word a meaning that is different from its ordinary meaning. It is bad draftsmanship, I think, to call a man an agent who is trading on his own account.
Mr. A. K. MACLEAljr: I was going to suggest that the first part of that clause be amended to say:
Every manufacturer, importer or dealer.
I should like to have the sense of the committee on that amendment. It might
protect a very small seller of fertilizers in the event of some violation of the Act by him.
I do not see why you want the word " dealer " there. A dealer is a retailer.
I suppose the idea is that the ultimate consumer shall have protection of real value.

Yes. I hesitate to amend the section. I am satisfied that it will be all right. I know the objection, which I suggested myself, can very validly be raised. On the whole I would prefer leaving the section as it is.

Could not a covering clause be put at the end, saying that this shall not have application to sales of, say, 25 lb. and under? That would cover the case where the owner of a garden went to his florist or grocer and bought some of this stuff; he would then be relying upon the reputation of the person from whom he was buying.
After all, the administration of the Act is in the hands of officials of the department, and any prosecutions would have to be conducted by them. I would ask the Committee to let the section stand.

Departmental officials are sometimes very meddlesome. I know that prosecutions are going on in my constituency at the present time at the instance of an official who is going through the little stores and inducing people to sell a twenty-five cent package of talcum powder, or something of that kind, without affixing the necessary stamp. A case occurred the other" day where a constable went into a small country store and induced the little girl who was in charge to sell him a package of talcum powder without the stamp .on it. The proprietor was not present. The first he knew of it was through a summons. This is the way the Inland Revenue Department is prosecuting people through officials whose sense of duty is aroused by the prospect of pocketing a portion of the fines that may be imposed on unwitting offenders.
I think revenue laws must be rigidly enforced. The cases are not analogous.

The law should
be enforced by responsible officers.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
May I ask the minister if he has many more amendments?
There are several.

Really I feel that I have not done justice to the clause that has just been passed. I am not satisfied with it; neither, I think, is the minister. If we have to consider a number of clauses of the same nature I do not think we should attempt it to-night. We want to pass a Bill which satisfies us, and I do not like the principle that we can pass more or less slip-shod legislation and depend upon the good sense of the officers of the Crown to use with discretion the weapon placed in their hands. As a rule I presume they do use discretion, but not always; they are frail men like ourselves. It is our duty to pass the best legislation we can, and it is the duty of the officers of the Crown to put that into effect to the best of their ability. It seems to me that it would be better to have this Bill reprinted and distributed.

I must confess that I feel it is in a sense unfair to the Committee to offer so many lengthy amendments without their having had an opportunity to consider them. That was my feeling at the beginning, and as the hon. gentleman has expressed a desire that the Bill be reprinted before proceeding further, I do not feel that I can refuse his request. So I move that we rise and report progress.
Progress reported.
On the order: Third reading of Bill No. 42, to amend the Weights and Measures Act:

Mr. Chairman, this Bill, it will be remembered, was considered yesterday and we had quite a lengthy discussion on section 7, which provides a money penalty for short weight delivery. The leader of the Opposition suggested the possibility or probability of malicious proceedings being taken against merchants or dealers selling short weight. As I explained yesterday, it is not possible to secure a conviction except through officers of the department being in a store and establishing, right at the moment of sale or immediately afterwards, the fact of the article being short in weight. If an article is purchased and is taken home, and then brought back to the store, and the purchaser asks to be relieved of his purchase
['Mr. Sinclair.] 1	i| !	!!! 1 M
upon the ground of short weight, it could never be established in any court. However, after hearing the remarks made by the leader of the Opposition and the member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow), I concluded that possibly the Act might be open to abuse, and I wish to amend the clause by adding these words:-
No proceedings shall be taken under the provisions of this section except with the consent of the minister.
The hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) yesterday amended this clause by providing penalties for second and subsequent offences, and in the drafting of it he used figures, and I should like to have those expressed in extenso. I move:
That the order for the third reading of Bill No. 42, to amend the Weights and Measures Act, be now discharged and that the said Bill be referred back to the Committee of the Whole with power to amend the same by striking out clause 7 of the said Bill and substituting therefor the following clause:
"7. The following section is inserted immediately after section sixty-one of the said Act:-
"61. (a) Notwithstanding any of the provisions of the Criminal Code, any person who sells, delivers or causes to be sold or delivered, anything by weight, measure or number, short of the quantity ordered purchased, shall be guilty of an offence and liable to a fine not exceeding twenty-five dollars for the first offence and to a fine not exceeding one hundred dollars for any subsequent offence. No proceedings shall be taken under the provisions of this section except with the consent of the minister."
Motion agreed to, and the House thereupon went into Committee, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

I move to amend clause 7 of the Bill by striking out all the words after the word "Act" in the second line of the said clause and substituting the following:
61. (a) Notwithstanding any of the provisions of the Criminal Code, any person who sells, delivers or causes to be sold or delivered, anything by weight, measure or number, short of the quantity ordered purchased, shall be guilty of an offence and liable to a fine not exceeding twenty-five dollars for the first offence and to a fine not exceeding one hundred dollars for any subsequent offence. No proceedings shall be taken under the provisions of this section except with the consent of the minister.

I wish further to support my objection to this Bill. I am very glad that the minister is making it considerably better by throwing this safeguard around it, that a responsible minister will have to give his consent; and I suppose he will be satisfied with nothing short of substantial evidence before he will give his authority to the proceedings. The minister

states that the person who gets the short weight is expected to come back to the store and deliver up the goods and say that they are short weight. There is nothing in the Bill to that effect.
No.

What would happen in many cases is an entirely different proceeding. The minister is measuring the capacity of some magistrates of this country by his own honest idea of things and thinks that what he would not do himself will not be done by a magistrate. Magistrates will do the most extraordinary things. Let me point out to the minister what might happen in many cases and what will happen under this Bill if magistrates get the authority. Mr. A is dealing with a grocery where he gets his groceries from day to day, and he has a little scale in his house with which he weighs everything he buys. He runs into debt to the merchant, and one day his little girl goes to the store for, say, ten pounds of sugar and a pound of tea and the merchant says: I will not give it to you because I am tired of giving your father goods, as he is not paying for what he gets. She goes home and immediately they discover that the last pound of tea and the last pound of sugar were short in weight, and they at once proceed to lay an information against that man before some stupid magistrate who is quite willing to accept their evidence as against that of the merchant. The merchant will say: I do not remember, but according to the custom of the trade and my custom I believe I gave that girl one pound of tea and one pound of sugar; but they will swear positively with spite and malice against that man who refused to give them goods. Even if the magistrate were fairly disposed to be honest, as I will give him credit for being, what has he before him? He has the sworn testimony, perhaps of a whole family, that the weight was short, while the merchant can do nothing except depend upon the custom of the trade and his custom in dealing with people. That is the position into which this section is putting every honest man 'who is doing business.
I hope my amendment will prevent that.

Amendment agreed to.
